content.question: You hit a URL in your browser. What VERB did you just use without knowing it?

content.prompt: Match each status code to its meaning — which one means "created successfully"?

content.text: HTTP is a conversation between a waiter (client) and kitchen (server). The METHOD is what you ask ("I'd like to ORDER" = POST, "What's on the menu?" = GET). The STATUS CODE is the kitchen's reply ("Here you go" = 200, "We don't have that" = 404). HEADERS are side notes on the order slip — "no nuts" (Accept: application/json), "table 5" (Authorization: Bearer token).

content.annotation: Every HTTP exchange has a METHOD (the verb — GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), a URL (the address), HEADERS (metadata like Accept and Content-Type), and an optional BODY (the payload). GET/DELETE typically have no body. POST/PUT carry a body. Headers travel in BOTH directions — request and response.

content.setup:
POST /users
Content-Type: application/json
Body: {"name": "Subham"}
→ Response: 201 Created
content.modification: What if you send POST without Content-Type header?
content.question: What likely happens?
content.explanation: The server doesn't know how to parse the body without Content-Type. It returns 415 — "I don't understand this format." Always set Content-Type when sending a body.

content.label: GET vs POST — when to use which:
content.codeA:
GET /users/1
(No body, safe, idempotent)
→ 200 + user data
content.codeB:
POST /users
Body: {"name": "New User"}
(Has body, NOT idempotent)
→ 201 + created user
content.question: Why can't you use GET to create a resource?
options: GET has no body to send data
content.explanation: GET has no body (as shown in the request anatomy — "empty for GET") and is idempotent like the kitchen answering "What's on the menu?" the same way every time. POST is "I'd like to ORDER" — it creates something new each time. Using GET to create would break both the no-body rule and the idempotent contract.

content.prompt: Describe what a client sends in an HTTP request.
content.sentence: A client sends a _____ (the verb like GET or POST), a _____ (the address), _____ (metadata like Content-Type), and an optional _____ (the data payload).

content.text: Every REST Assured test maps directly to this anatomy:
content.code:
given()                          // headers, auth, params
  .header("Accept", "application/json")
.when()                          // method + URL
  .get("/users/1")
.then()                          // validate response
  .statusCode(200);
content.note: REST Assured's DSL is literally "given this request setup, when I call this method, then I expect this response." You now know what each piece means at the HTTP level.
